title: Antimicrobial stewardship and communicable disease surveillance
blurb: Support safe antimicrobial use under NICE NG15, take the right samples at the right time, and know when infections must be notified or escalated.
question: An inpatient with suspected urinary tract infection is prescribed oral antibiotics. She is alert, with a NEWS2 score of 1, and no sample has been taken. What should the nurse do before giving the first dose?

teach.body: Antimicrobial resistance happens when organisms adapt so that medicines which used to kill them no longer work. Every course of antimicrobials, needed or not, adds selection pressure. Antimicrobial stewardship is the organised effort to use antimicrobials only when needed, at the right dose and duration, and to review them. NICE NG15 asks prescribers to weigh the risk of resistance for the individual patient AND for the population as a whole.

teach.caption: NG15 1.1.26-1.1.39: clinical assessment, samples, documentation, review.

teach.h: NICE NG15 recommendations nurses act on
head: Rec
What it says
rows: Hospital: take microbiological samples before prescribing, review when results arrive
Document the reason for prescribing or not, and the planned duration
No immediate antimicrobial for a likely self-limiting condition
Options: self-care, back-up (delayed) prescription, non-drug measures
Weigh harms, including allergies and the risk of C. difficile
Consider reviewing IV antimicrobials at 48-72 hours, including switch to oral

teach.h: Samples first, but never delay urgent treatment
teach.body: In hospital, taking a sample before the first dose lets the team narrow or stop treatment once results return. That does not mean waiting. For a person at high risk from sepsis (NEWS2 7 or more), NICE NG253 expects blood cultures with the first bloods and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of the NEWS2 score. Take the culture quickly, then give the antibiotic on time.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Obi and Ahmed
teach.body: Ahmed, 66, is on day 3 of IV co-amoxiclav for pneumonia. He is now afebrile, eating and drinking, and his blood culture has grown a sensitive organism. Obi recognises the 48-72 hour review point and asks the prescriber to review a switch to oral antibiotics using the culture result, as NG15 1.1.39 suggests. An unnecessary IV line is also an infection risk, so a timely switch may allow the cannula to come out.

Surveillance means systematically collecting and acting on infection data to spot outbreaks early. In England, registered medical practitioners must notify the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) of a notifiable disease on clinical suspicion, without waiting for laboratory confirmation. Urgent cases are telephoned to the local health protection team within 24 hours, and all cases are reported within 3 days. Nurses who suspect one inform the doctor and the IPC team promptly.

teach.caption: MRSA and C. difficile are major IPC concerns managed with the IPC team, but they are not notifiable diseases.

teach.text: Do not confuse 'notifiable disease' with 'common hospital infection'. MRSA and C. difficile matter enormously for IPC, but they are not on the UKHSA notifiable list. Measles and invasive group A strep are, and are notified urgently on suspicion.

items: Stewardship protects the individual and the population from resistance (NG15).
Hospital: samples before the first dose, then review when results arrive; urgent sepsis antibiotics are not delayed.
No immediate antibiotics for self-limiting illness; consider back-up prescriptions and give safety-netting advice.
Consider reviewing IV antimicrobials at 48-72 hours and switching to oral where possible.
Notifiable diseases are notified on suspicion; urgent ones by phone within 24 hours, all within 3 days.

summary: You can now explain antimicrobial resistance and apply NICE NG15 to sampling, prescribing decisions and 48-72 hour reviews. You can also recognise notifiable diseases and respond to a suspected outbreak.

A.q: Rose, 70, an inpatient, has new dysuria and frequency. She is alert with a NEWS2 score of 1. Oral nitrofurantoin is prescribed. What should the nurse do before the first dose?
options: Give the dose and send a urine sample tomorrow
Withhold the antibiotic until the urine culture result is back from the lab
Ask the doctor to prescribe IV antibiotics as a precaution
Obtain a urine sample, then give the antibiotic without delay
A.why: NICE NG15 1.1.27: in hospital, take microbiological samples before prescribing an antimicrobial and review when results are available. The dose should then be given promptly.

whyNot.0: A sample taken after antibiotics may be falsely negative and cannot guide review.
whyNot.1: Waiting days for culture delays treatment of a symptomatic infection.
whyNot.2: IV treatment is not indicated for a well patient who can take oral medicines.

A.q: Callum, 29, has a 3-day runny nose, sore throat and mild cough. He is well with normal observations and asks the practice nurse prescriber for antibiotics. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Prescribe a 5-day course of amoxicillin to be safe
Refer him to the GP for a second opinion on antibiotics
Prescribe antibiotics and advise him to stop taking them once he feels better
Explain antibiotics will not help, and give safety-netting advice
A.why: NG15 1.1.33: do not issue an immediate antimicrobial prescription to a patient likely to have a self-limiting condition. Discuss the likely course and what to do if he worsens (1.1.31).

whyNot.0: An antibiotic for a self-limiting viral illness adds harms and resistance without benefit.
whyNot.1: A competent nurse prescriber can manage this; referral delays clear advice.
whyNot.2: Prescribing for a self-limiting illness goes against NG15, and stopping early is not advised.

A.q: Which statement best describes antimicrobial resistance?
options: Organisms adapt so that antimicrobials no longer work against them
Patients gradually become allergic to antibiotics after repeated courses
The body's immune system stops responding to antibiotics
Antibiotics lose strength if stored at the wrong temperature
A.why: Resistance is a property of the organism: microbes adapt so the medicine no longer kills or inhibits them, driven by antimicrobial use.

whyNot.1: Allergy is an immune reaction in the patient, not resistance in the organism.
whyNot.2: Antibiotics act on microbes, not on the immune system.
whyNot.3: Poor storage reduces potency of a medicine but is not antimicrobial resistance.

B.q: Ahmed, 66, is on day 3 of IV co-amoxiclav for pneumonia. He is afebrile, eating and drinking, and his blood culture shows a sensitive organism. What should the nurse do?
options: Continue IV treatment until the full 7-day course is complete as planned
Ask the prescriber to review an oral switch using his results
Stop the antibiotic, as he is now afebrile
Request a broader-spectrum IV agent to be safe
B.why: NG15 1.1.39: consider reviewing IV antimicrobials at 48-72 hours, including response and microbiology results, to decide whether to continue and whether to switch to oral.

whyNot.0: Continuing IV without review ignores the 48-72 hour review and keeps an unnecessary line in.
whyNot.2: Nurses do not stop a prescribed antibiotic; the prescriber decides on duration.
whyNot.3: A sensitive organism means narrowing, not broadening, is appropriate.

B.q: June, 72, has NEWS2 8 and suspected sepsis from a chest infection. Blood cultures and lactate have been taken and IV antibiotics are prescribed. The doctor wants to wait for a sputum sample, which June cannot produce yet. What should the nurse do?
options: Wait for the sputum sample before giving the first antibiotic dose
Give oral antibiotics while waiting for the sputum
Give the antibiotic now, within 1 hour of the NEWS2 score
Recalculate NEWS2 in 4 hours, then decide
B.why: NEWS2 7 or more is high risk; NG253 requires broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of the score. Blood cultures are taken; further samples must not delay treatment.

whyNot.0: Delaying antibiotics for a sputum sample in high-risk sepsis increases the risk of death.
whyNot.1: High-risk sepsis needs IV, not oral, antibiotics.
whyNot.3: High-risk patients have NEWS2 recalculated every 30 minutes, and treatment is not deferred.

B.q: A practice nurse prescriber decides an immediate antibiotic is not needed for Mia's likely self-limiting chest infection. Which alternative does NG15 suggest discussing?
options: A back-up (delayed) prescription with clear advice
A lower dose of antibiotic for a shorter time
An antibiotic started now but stopped early
A course of a different, broader-spectrum antibiotic agent
B.why: NG15 1.1.34 lists self-care with over-the-counter preparations, back-up (delayed) prescribing and non-drug measures as options when immediate prescribing is not appropriate.

whyNot.1: Under-dosing is not a stewardship option and may promote resistance.
whyNot.2: Starting an unnecessary course is the immediate prescribing NG15 advises against.
whyNot.3: Broader-spectrum agents increase resistance and C. difficile risk.

C.q: Within 24 hours, three patients in the same six-bed bay develop sudden vomiting and diarrhoea. None was admitted with these symptoms. What is the most important action for the nurse in charge?
options: Wait for stool results before taking any action
Start antidiarrhoeal medicines for all three patients
Move each patient to a different bay to dilute the spread
Inform the IPC team promptly about a possible outbreak
C.why: A cluster of new-onset diarrhoea and vomiting suggests an outbreak. Contact precautions and prompt IPC team involvement allow cohorting, cleaning and possible bay closure.

whyNot.0: Waiting for results allows further spread; action starts on clinical suspicion.
whyNot.1: Antidiarrhoeals are not an IPC measure and may be harmful in infective diarrhoea.
whyNot.2: Moving patients spreads the organism to more bays.

C.q: Mia, 4, attends a GP practice with high fever, cough, conjunctivitis and a spreading rash. She is unvaccinated and the GP suspects measles. How must the disease be notified?
options: After laboratory confirmation, within 3 days
On suspicion, urgently by phone to the health protection team
By letter to the local authority at the end of the working week
When a second case is found in the same nursery
C.why: Notifiable diseases are notified on clinical suspicion without waiting for confirmation; urgent ones such as measles are phoned to the UKHSA health protection team within 24 hours.

whyNot.0: Notification must not wait for laboratory confirmation, and measles is urgent.
whyNot.2: Notification goes to UKHSA, and urgent cases are phoned within 24 hours.
whyNot.3: Each suspected case is notifiable; there is no requirement for a second case.

C.q: Victor, 81, has had 5 days of clindamycin for cellulitis. He now has four episodes of watery diarrhoea in 12 hours and is in a four-bed bay. What is the best initial plan?
options: Isolate him, send a stool sample and ask for an antibiotic review
Give loperamide and monitor in the bay
Notify UKHSA by phone today, as C. difficile is a notifiable disease
Continue clindamycin and recheck stools in 48 hours
C.why: Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea suggests possible C. difficile: isolate with contact precautions and soap-and-water hand hygiene, send a stool sample and ask the prescriber to review the antibiotic (NG15 1.1.35 highlights C. difficile risk).

whyNot.1: Antidiarrhoeals are avoided in suspected infective diarrhoea, and he needs isolation.
whyNot.2: C. difficile is not on the UKHSA notifiable list; it is managed through local IPC and surveillance.
whyNot.3: Continuing the antibiotic without review and delaying action risks harm and spread.

reteach.title: Antibiotics are a shared resource
reteach.question: If every unnecessary course weakens antibiotics for everyone, how do you decide when one is truly needed?

blocks.body: Start smart: assess properly, take samples first in hospital, and do not treat self-limiting illness. Then focus: review at 48-72 hours with the results, and stop, narrow or switch to oral. Each step protects the patient in front of you and keeps antibiotics working for the next one.

children.label: Cultures and IV within 1 hour
children.sub: do not delay for other samples

blocks.text: Samples before antibiotics, yes, but samples must never delay antibiotics in high-risk sepsis.

explain.body: Organisms adapt so antimicrobials no longer work. Unnecessary or poorly targeted use drives it, so NG15 asks prescribers to consider the risk to the individual and the population.

items.label: risk of resistance for this patient

test.q: Which practice most directly drives antimicrobial resistance?
options: Taking blood cultures before antibiotics
Prescribing antibiotics for self-limiting viral illness
Reviewing IV antibiotics at 48-72 hours
Switching from IV to oral antibiotics once the patient improves
test.why: Unnecessary antimicrobial use creates selection pressure for resistant organisms without benefit.

whyNot.0: Samples allow targeted treatment and support stewardship.
whyNot.2: Review is a stewardship measure that reduces unnecessary use.
whyNot.3: Switching to oral when appropriate is part of good stewardship.

explain.body: Hospital: take samples before prescribing and review once results arrive (NG15 1.1.27). High-risk sepsis: blood cultures with first bloods, antibiotics within 1 hour (NG253).

test.q: When should microbiological samples be taken for a hospital inpatient with suspected infection?
options: Before the antimicrobial is prescribed
After the third dose of antibiotic
When the course has finished
If the first antibiotic course fails to work
test.why: NG15 1.1.27: for patients in hospital with suspected infection, take samples before prescribing an antimicrobial.

whyNot.1: After doses, cultures may be falsely negative.
whyNot.2: End-of-course samples cannot guide the treatment choice.
whyNot.3: Waiting for failure delays targeted treatment.

explain.body: Include response and microbiology results, then decide whether to continue, stop, narrow or switch IV to oral (NG15 1.1.39).

test.q: At what point does NICE NG15 suggest reviewing intravenous antimicrobial prescriptions?
options: Within 24 hours
After 7 days
After 5 days
At 48-72 hours
test.why: NG15 1.1.39: consider reviewing IV antimicrobial prescriptions at 48-72 hours in all settings.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is usually too early for culture results to guide review.
whyNot.1: 7 days is far beyond the recommended review point.
whyNot.2: 5 days is later than the recommended review point.

explain.body: Registered medical practitioners notify UKHSA on suspicion. Urgent: phone within 24 hours. All cases: report within 3 days. Examples: measles, invasive group A strep, TB. Not notifiable: MRSA, C. difficile.

items.label: Notify, do not wait for lab

test.q: Which of these is a notifiable disease in England?
options: MRSA colonisation
Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI)
Invasive group A streptococcal disease
Seasonal influenza
test.why: Invasive group A streptococcal disease is on the UKHSA notifiable diseases list.

whyNot.0: MRSA is not a notifiable disease.
whyNot.1: C. difficile is not on the notifiable list.
whyNot.3: Seasonal influenza is not notifiable; influenza of zoonotic origin is.
